steps.title: Optimize Sample Concentration and Absorbance
steps.instruction: Adjust sample concentration and absorbance to ensure reproducible results and reader compatibility.

substeps.instruction: Dilute samples with Sample Buffer or concentrate using an Amicon centrifuge concentrator (10,000 MWCO) so that the absorbance decrease is between 0.008 and 0.1/min.
If initial absorbance is > 1.2 (e.g., erythrocyte lysates), dilute with Sample Buffer until absorbance is lowered.
If samples contain high levels of GSSG or NADPH consuming enzymes, remove GSSG via dialysis or gel filtration, or perform a blank without GSSG to assess nonspecific oxidation of NADPH.

steps.title: Initiate Reactions
steps.instruction: Start the enzymatic reactions by adding 50 µl of NADPH to all active wells.

substeps.instruction: Add NADPH as quickly as possible

steps.title: Mix Plate
steps.instruction: Carefully shake the 96-well plate for a few seconds to mix the contents.

steps.title: Measure Absorbance
steps.instruction: Read the absorbance at 340 nm using a plate reader once every minute to obtain at least 5 time points.

substeps.instruction: Verify that the initial absorbance of sample wells is between 0.5 and 1.2

steps.title: Calculate GR Activity
steps.instruction: Determine the glutathione reductase (GR) activity based on the change in absorbance (ΔA 340) per minute.

substeps.instruction: Determine the ΔA 340/min by either plotting absorbance vs. time to find the slope of the linear portion or by calculating the absolute change between two points on the linear portion.
Subtract the ΔA 340/min of the background/non-enzymatic wells from the sample well rate.
Calculate GR activity using the NADPH extinction coefficient of 0.00373 µM⁻¹ (adjusted for a 0.6 cm pathlength from the actual coefficient of 0.00622 µM⁻¹cm⁻¹).
Define one unit as the amount of enzyme causing the oxidation of 1.0 nmol of NADPH to NADP+ per minute at 25ºC.

description: Background or Non-enzymatic Wells - add 120 µl of Assay Buffer and 20 µl of GSSG to three wells.
